title: AI Outbound Calling: How Modern Sales Teams Use AI to Book More Meetings Without Burning Out SDRs
summary: Discover how AI outbound calling combines intelligent dialing, AI voice agents, and real time coaching to help SDRs book more meetings and scale outbound sales.
body_text: A typical SDR spends hours dialing numbers, leaving voicemails, navigating receptionists, logging call outcomes, updating CRM records, switching between browser tabs, and hearing "I'm busy" dozens of times before finding someone willing to have a conversation. Even highly motivated representatives eventually feel the mental fatigue that comes with repeating the same routine hundreds of times every week. Bottom line: it’s called the burnout factor, and it’s very common, regardless of whether you’re a sales rep or anyone else working a job. We’re all humans, and we get tired of the mundane processes , if there aren’t any smart solutions to escalate the overall output. To keep things on point, sales managers responsible for heading different SDR teams see the symptoms everywhere. How so? For starters, they’ve been there during the early stages of their career, alluding to the fact that they’ve faced similar challenges and have overcome them efficiently. Particularly speaking about the overall slow pace, there are a lot of things that impact stuff in a loop shape. Normally, we see the hiring process taking longer than expected. Then you have to factor in the ramp time, as in training those reps and bringing them up to speed, in terms of whatever products they’re going to be selling, scripts, max time to spend on each call and vice versa. There’s a lot that could go into the training factor. But to keep things on point, if you are looking for budget based hiring, then expert SDRs are definitely going to come onboard with a higher payroll requirement. Usually, businesses want to keep the expense side of things low, so budget underlines decision making process and impacts how things eventually pan out. At some point, simply asking people to work harder stops producing better results. This is exactly why AI outbound calling has become one of the biggest conversations in modern revenue teams. It is changing far more than the way calls are placed. It is changing how outbound sales is designed from the ground up. Rather than asking one SDR to manually complete one hundred phone calls every day, companies can now let intelligent systems handle repetitive conversations while human sellers spend more time speaking with prospects who already have genuine interest. That changes everything in a lot of ways. Sales teams are discovering that AI powered voice calling for sales creates opportunities that were almost impossible only a few years ago. Large prospect lists become manageable. Response times shrink dramatically. Representatives spend less time performing repetitive work and more time building relationships that close revenue. The conversation has moved far beyond simple automation. Modern platforms now combine Intelligent phone dialing and calling systems , Automated call handling and routing , Real time call coaching and guidance , and highly capable AI voice agents and virtual sales assistants into one connected outbound workflow. Those capabilities allow organizations to scale conversations without sacrificing quality. That naturally leads to an important question many revenue leaders are asking. How do modern sales teams use AI to book more meetings without burning out SDRs? The answer has very little to do with replacing people. More robust organizations are giving repetitive activities to AI while allowing experienced sales professionals to spend their energy where humans create the greatest value. Throughout this series, we'll walk through every stage of that process, beginning with the biggest reason traditional outbound prospecting struggles today. Why Traditional Outbound Is Becoming Harder Every Year? That’s a very common question that circulates the industry way more frequently than you’d anticipate. Outbound sales have never been easy. With a higher call volume, and a naturally ocurring low cold call conversion rate, a lot has to go into the planning and exrcution phase behind each call. On top of that, SDRs are on a time crunch, so there’s only a specific amount of time they can allocate to the call + conversion ratio. Does the time spent on research part count? No, not really. Your manager may acknowledge the fact that you, as an SDR, do due diligence on pulling up research concerning prospects’ pain points, but at the end of the day, it’s the conversion that matters. And it also impacts your sales closing goals, quota and overall incentivization system. Low closure will eventually result in a lay off. But that’s also part of the game because SDRs end up learning stuff before they start applying for a new role in another company. Cold calling has always required persistence, resilience, confidence, and a willingness to hear rejection over and over again. The difference today is that nearly every obstacle has become larger. Buyers receive more emails than ever. Phone numbers are screened. Spam filters continue improving. Receptionists receive better training. Decision makers protect their calendars much more aggressively than they did several years ago. All of that means SDRs have to work significantly harder just to create the same number of conversations. The frustrating part is that most of an SDR's work never involves selling. Think about what happens during a typical workday. A representative opens the CRM, reviews a prospect list, copies contact information, launches the dialer, waits for the connection, reaches voicemail, leaves a message, updates the record, schedules another follow up, moves to the next prospect, and repeats that cycle dozens of times. Hours disappear before meaningful conversations even begin. The workload feels productive because there is constant activity. Unfortunately, activity and pipeline are very different things. Many organizations still evaluate SDR performance through numbers like daily dials or emails sent. More Activity Does Not Always Create More Pipeline Imagine two different SDRs. The first representative manually places one hundred calls throughout the day. The second representative spends almost the entire day speaking with qualified prospects because repetitive work has already been handled through AI outbound calling . Both employees worked eight hours. One generated activity. The other generated conversations. Revenue teams care about conversations. That difference becomes even larger once companies begin adopting AI powered voice calling for sales across multiple territories. Rather than increasing headcount every quarter, organizations can dramatically increase outbound capacity while allowing experienced sellers to spend their time on higher value interactions. That creates a healthier balance across the entire sales organization. Burnout Is Expensive Long Before Someone Resigns Burnout rarely happens overnight. It builds slowly. Representatives begin losing enthusiasm. Call quality becomes inconsistent. Follow ups become less personalized. Confidence slowly disappears. Managers spend more time coaching mindset than improving sales skills. Eventually many talented SDRs begin searching for another opportunity. Replacing them creates another round of recruiting, onboarding, product training, coaching sessions, and several months before new hires become fully productive. Every departure costs much more than another salary. Automated Call Handling and Routing Creates Faster Conversations, Not More Robotic Ones One of the biggest misconceptions about AI in outbound sales is that it simply places more phone calls. That would be a fairly small improvement. Modern Automated call handling and routing changes almost every stage of the outbound process before a sales representative even joins the conversation. Think about how much time disappears during a normal calling session. An SDR dials the number, but the prospect does not answer. The call reaches voicemail. Another number connects to a receptionist. The receptionist transfers the call. The line disconnects. Someone answers but asks for a callback. The representative updates the CRM before moving to the next contact. None of those activities generate revenue. They simply consume time. Modern AI handles those repetitive interactions automatically, allowing sales representatives to spend far more of their day having conversations with people who are ready to engage. The improvement goes much deeper than placing calls faster. Every interaction becomes part of an intelligent workflow that decides what should happen next without requiring manual intervention. AI Understands What Happens During Every Call Traditional dialers treated every phone call exactly the same. A number was dialed; someone answered, or they did not. The representative handled everything from that point onward. Today's Intelligent phone dialing and calling systems understand what is happening throughout the conversation. They recognize different call outcomes almost immediately. For example, the system can identify several situations within seconds. • A voicemail answers the phone • A receptionist or gatekeeper answers • The prospect answers directly • The number is disconnected • The prospect requests another call later • The conversation qualifies for an immediate transfer Every one of those outcomes triggers a different action automatically. There is no need for the SDR to stop, make decisions, update notes, or remember follow up schedules. The system keeps the workflow moving while the representative stays focused on conversations that matter. Intelligent Routing Keeps Buyers Moving Without Friction Think about the customer experience for a moment. Nobody enjoys repeating the same information three different times after being transferred between departments. It creates frustration before the sales conversation even begins. Modern Automated call handling and routing solve this problem through intelligent decision making. Once AI understands the buyer's responses, it can immediately determine where that conversation should go next. For example, someone asking pricing questions may need an Account Executive. Another example could be someone asking about implementation timelines, who could speak with a Customer Success specialist. Because the conversation history moves with the prospect, the next person joins fully prepared. The buyer does not have to repeat everything from the beginning. That creates a far smoother buying experience while helping internal teams spend less time gathering information that has already been collected. AI Creates Better Timing Across Your Sales Team Timing has always been one of the hardest parts of outbound prospecting. A prospect may answer while your SDR is already speaking with someone else. Someone requests a callback at exactly the wrong time. An inbound lead arrives while representatives are occupied making outbound calls. Without automation, opportunities can disappear surprisingly quickly. Modern AI solves much of that scheduling complexity. When conversations qualify, meetings can be booked automatically. When prospects request another conversation, callbacks are scheduled instantly. When someone becomes sales ready, AI can transfer them immediately to an available representative. That creates a much faster buying experience without forcing SDRs to juggle multiple conversations at once. Why Real Time Call Coaching and Guidance Produces Better Meetings Most sales coaching happens after the conversation has already ended. Managers review call recordings. They point out missed questions. They suggest stronger responses. Everyone agrees to improve next time. That approach certainly helps, but it comes after the opportunity has already passed. Modern Real time call coaching and guidance changes that process completely. Representatives receive helpful recommendations while the conversation is still happening. Imagine speaking with a prospect who mentions hiring twenty new SDRs next quarter. AI immediately recognizes a buying signal. Without interrupting the conversation, it surfaces recommended discovery questions, relevant customer stories, pricing information, and objection handling suggestions directly on the representative's screen. The SDR stays present in the conversation while receiving guidance that normally comes months later during coaching sessions. That shortens learning curves dramatically. Every Representative Has Access to Your Best Sales Playbook One reason experienced salespeople outperform new hires is simple. They have seen hundreds of conversations; they recognize patterns. On top of that, they also know which questions uncover buying intent. New representatives need months to develop those instincts. AI helps close that experience gap much faster. Rather than relying entirely on memory, representatives receive recommendations built from successful conversations across the organization. That creates greater consistency without making conversations sound scripted. Every SDR benefits from knowledge that previously lived only inside the minds of top performers. Coaching Happens While Confidence Is Still High One overlooked advantage of Real time call coaching and guidance is psychological. Cold calling can be emotionally exhausting. After several difficult conversations, even experienced SDRs begin questioning themselves. That uncertainty affects confidence, ultimately affecting the overall communication pattern. In that order, to render massive support, AI provides steady support throughout the day. If a prospect raises a pricing concern, the representative immediately sees recommended responses. If a competitor is mentioned, relevant competitive positioning appears automatically. If discovery questions have been skipped, the system reminds the representative before moving toward scheduling. Those small moments of assistance reduce hesitation. Representatives feel more prepared because they know guidance is available throughout every conversation. That confidence often leads to more natural conversations and stronger meeting quality. Better Coaching Creates Better Data Every conversation teaches something. Buyers ask new questions. Competitors introduce new messaging. Market conditions change. Traditional coaching depends on managers manually identifying those trends. AI analyzes thousands of conversations continuously. Patterns begin appearing much sooner. Sales leaders can quickly identify which objections appear most frequently, which messaging resonates with different buyer personas, and which questions produce the highest meeting conversion rates. That creates a feedback loop where coaching continuously improves because it reflects current buyer behavior rather than assumptions made several months ago. What's the Best AI Outbound Calling Strategy for 2026? This is one of the most common questions revenue leaders are asking today. What's the best AI outbound calling strategy for 2026? Many organizations assume success comes from buying the newest platform with the most impressive feature list. Technology certainly matters; tt simply should not be the starting point. The strongest outbound programs begin with strategy and allow technology to support that strategy. Companies that build a thoughtful outbound process create remarkable results because AI amplifies practices that already work. A successful strategy combines people, AI, data, and workflow into one coordinated system. Build Highly Focused Prospect Segments Large prospect lists often look impressive on paper. They rarely produce impressive conversations. Group prospects according to shared characteristics, business priorities, hiring activity, technologies, company size, and buying signals. The more relevant your messaging becomes, the more naturally AI conversations sound. This is one area where personalization continues outperforming volume. Train AI Around Conversations Rather Than Scripts Many organizations still think in terms of scripts. Buyers rarely follow scripts. Every conversation takes unexpected turns. Train your AI around conversation paths, common objections, qualifying questions, and buying signals. That flexibility allows AI voice agents and virtual sales assistants to respond naturally while keeping conversations moving toward the next logical step. Keep Humans Involved at High Value Moments AI performs repetitive work exceptionally well. Relationship building still belongs to people. Allow AI to qualify prospects, answer common questions, schedule meetings, and gather context. Bring experienced salespeople into conversations where buying decisions become more complex. That partnership creates a stronger experience for both buyers and sales teams. Connect AI With Your Existing Sales Stack One reason AI adoption has accelerated so quickly is that companies no longer need to rebuild their technology ecosystem from scratch. Many AI calling platforms connect directly with CRMs, sales engagement platforms, calendar software, conversation intelligence tools, and analytics systems. This naturally answers another question many organizations ask. How to implement AI calling within your existing sales engagement platform? A couple of things that you can do for a head start. Take them as a general guideline, because we’d want you to improvise for the best long term results… Begin with one outbound team. Connect AI to your CRM. Import one carefully segmented prospect list. Test conversation flows. Review call recordings. Measure outcomes. Refine messaging. Expand gradually after performance becomes predictable. Rolling out AI in phases produces better adoption than attempting a company wide deployment overnight. Appointing a Technology Champion: Is It a Good Decision? Technology champions are bunch of people that are well-versed in any software, it’s overall features and how to use the latest technology. Even if the program comes with tons of automation and self explanatory AI tech stack, sales teams do need training from someone who has hands on experience. A “techie” could be a nominated person from within your company, or they could be someone from outside. In the latter case, external support comes from the same company you bought the software from. Either they do it for free through one or two online meetings, or they charge you extra. If budget is a major concern, then go for an in-house technology champion who has prior experience with similar software etc. Ultimately, it’s your decision, so do whatever it takes to reduce ramp time for the entire team. Measure Business Outcomes Rather Than Call Volume Modern outbound organizations no longer celebrate activity for its own sake. Revenue leaders want conversations that become pipeline. Eventually, it becomes revenue. That means performance reviews should move beyond simple dialing metrics. When leadership begins asking What metrics prove AI outbound calling improves sales performance? , the strongest answers usually include held meetings, qualified opportunities, conversion rates, pipeline contribution, sales cycle length, and revenue generated. Those measurements tell a much more complete story than daily call volume ever could. Confident SDRs Burn Out Less, Here's How Trellus Helps One of the biggest problems with traditional sales coaching is timing. Most coaching happens after the call is over. A manager listens to recordings, points out missed opportunities, shares feedback, and hopes the representative remembers it during the next conversation. Valuable advice arrives after the opportunity has already passed. Modern Real time call coaching and guidance works very differently. Platforms like Trellus provide live coaching while the conversation is happening. Rather than waiting for a weekly review session, representatives receive contextual suggestions the moment they need them. Imagine a prospect asking about pricing, mentioning a competitor, or raising an objection that commonly stalls deals. The platform can surface recommended talking points, objection handling guidance, relevant customer stories, or follow up questions without interrupting the conversation. The representative stays engaged with the buyer while receiving support that feels like having an experienced sales coach sitting beside them. This becomes especially valuable for newer SDRs who are still building confidence. Even experienced representatives have days when conversations do not go their way. Hearing repeated objections or dealing with multiple rejections can affect energy levels and decision making throughout the day. With intelligent guidance available during live conversations, hesitation begins to disappear. Representatives spend less time wondering what to say next and more time listening to the buyer. That creates smoother conversations, stronger discovery, and better qualified meetings. Over time, confidence grows naturally because every conversation becomes another learning opportunity rather than another stressful guessing exercise.

title: Measured in minutes: Helping customers reach the moments that matter most
body_text: When a flight was delayed out of Cleveland, Delta teams across Flight Operations, Airport Customer Service, In-Flight Service, OCC, Reservations & Care and TechOps quickly came together with one goal: keep customers moving safely and minimize impacts to their journey. Through proactive planning, seamless coordination and rapid execution, a ferry flight from DTW to JFK was diverted to recover the CLE-ATL flight, making up valuable time and helping customers stay on track — including the University of Akron softball team traveling to its first NCAA tournament appearance in program history. title: bioAffinity Technologies’ Quarterly CyPath® Lung Sales Double to New Record as Commercial Momentum Continues
summary: CyPath® Lung sales volume for Q2 2026 grows more than 200% year-over-year and 30% over record-breaking prior quarter Growth in Q2 driven by…...
body_text: bioAffinity Technologies’ Quarterly CyPath® Lung Sales Double to New Record as Commercial Momentum Continues July 07, 2026 8:46am EDT CyPath® Lung sales volume for Q2 2026 grows more than 200% year-over-year and 30% over record-breaking prior quarter Growth in Q2 driven by increasing utilization among existing clients and 155% increase in physician offices ordering CyPath® Lung as compared to Q2 2025 SAN ANTONIO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- bioAffinity Technologies, Inc. (Nasdaq: BIAF; BIAFW) , a biotechnology company focused on the need for noninvasive, accurate tests for the detection of early-stage lung cancer and other lung diseases, today announced continued acceleration in commercial sales for CyPath® Lung , its noninvasive lung cancer diagnostic, with more than 200% growth year-over-year. The number of tests sold in the second quarter of 2026 represents an increase of more than 30% over the first quarter of 2026 and more than 200% compared with the second quarter of 2025. "We are at the forefront of a positive change in clinical practice. We believe it is the result of expanding physician familiarity and accumulating clinical evidence as more patients are evaluated with CyPath® Lung and benefit from CyPath® Lung-guided care,” said Maria Zannes, President and Chief Executive Officer of bioAffinity Technologies. “The most encouraging trend goes beyond onboarding new practices — the fact is, physicians who try CyPath® Lung appreciate its benefits and continue to use it. Repeat utilization suggests the test is becoming part of routine clinical decision-making for patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules." The Company has now performed nearly 3,000 CyPath® Lung tests since commercial launch, reflecting growing physician adoption across pulmonology practices, lung nodule clinics, academic and community medical centers, and Veterans Affairs (VA) facilities. bioAffinity Technologies is executing a commercial strategy focused on increasing utilization of CyPath® Lung among existing clients, expanding its sales footprint in existing markets, strategically entering new markets, and building lasting relationships with physicians. "The number of patients diagnosed with indeterminate pulmonary nodules is expected to grow significantly over the next several years with expanded lung cancer screening and incidental findings from other procedures,” said Gordon Downie, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of bioAffinity Technologies. "The challenge is determining which patients require immediate invasive evaluation and which can be safely monitored. CyPath® Lung is designed to provide clinicians with an objective, noninvasive tool that complements imaging and helps them make more informed decisions while reducing unnecessary procedures and patient anxiety." In published patient case studies , CyPath® Lung has helped detect lung cancer at curative Stage 1A when risk stratification guidelines and other adjunct tests indicated low risk. Conversely, a negative CyPath® Lung result has spared patients with significant comorbidities from invasive, often risky procedures. In a recent interview , a CyPath® Lung patient describes the emotional impact of discovering a pulmonary nodule and explains why she appreciated having a noninvasive testing option. "I was petrified. I was scared to death," she recalls. "I was so thankful that CyPath® Lung was something that I could do that was noninvasive… I just want to shout it from the rafters." bioAffinity Technologies is advancing multiple initiatives that the Company believes will further expand the clinical impact of its proprietary technology platform. These include a large-scale longitudinal clinical study designed to generate additional validation data for CyPath® Lung, expansion into oncology by using CyPath® Lung to monitor lung cancer survivors after treatment, and an R&D pipeline that includes diagnostic tests for asthma and COPD that are designed to help guide personalized treatment with targeted therapies. “We are building on the success of CyPath® Lung to develop noninvasive tests designed to ensure asthma and COPD patients are matched with the most effective treatment for their type of lung disease,” Dr. Downie said. “We continue to develop our automated flow cytometry platform that supports an expanding number of diagnostic tests that we believe can lead to improved lung health for millions of people." The Company expects to report its financial results for the second quarter of 2026 in August. About CyPath® Lung CyPath® Lung by bioAffinity Technologies is a noninvasive test designed to improve the early detection of lung cancer in patients at high risk for the disease. CyPath® Lung uses advanced flow cytometry and proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) to identify cell populations in patient sputum that indicate malignancy. CyPath® Lung incorporates a fluorescent porphyrin that is preferentially taken up by cancer and cancer-related cells. In a published clinical trial of high-risk patients, CyPath® Lung demonstrated 92% sensitivity, 87% specificity, 88% accuracy and 99% negative predictive value (NPV) in detecting lung cancer in patients at high risk for the disease who had small indeterminate lung nodules less than 20 millimeters. The high NPV gives physicians greater confidence that a negative result is truly negative, potentially sparing patients from unnecessary invasive and costly procedures. CyPath® Lung is marketed as a Laboratory Developed Test (LDT) and is not intended for use as a sole diagnostic tool and should be considered alongside other clinical findings. About bioAffinity Technologies, Inc. bioAffinity Technologies, Inc. addresses the need for noninvasive diagnosis of early-stage cancer and other diseases of the lung and broad-spectrum cancer treatments. The Company’s first product, CyPath® Lung, is a noninvasive test that has shown high sensitivity, specificity and accuracy for the detection of early-stage lung cancer. CyPath® Lung is marketed as a Laboratory Developed Test (LDT) by Precision Pathology Laboratory Services, a subsidiary of bioAffinity Technologies. LDTs are overseen under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA), which are administered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. For more information, visit www.bioaffinitytech.com . Integrated with the CARTO ecosystem, the platform gives physicians greater versatility to tailor treatment based on patient anatomy and case complexity.i IRVINE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the Dual Energy THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF Platform (DE STSF), an integrated catheter ablation solution that enables electrophysiologists to deliver both radiofrequency (RF) and pulsed field (PF) energy through a single catheter.i Dual Energy THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF Catheter “The FDA approval of the Dual Energy THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF Platform is another important milestone in what has been an incredible pace of innovation for our business,” said Michael Bodner, Company Group Chair, Electrophysiology & Neurovascular, MedTech, Johnson & Johnson. “Our goal has always been to put the best possible technologies into physicians’ hands so they can treat increasingly complex cases with confidence. Following a successful introduction in Europe, we’re pleased to rapidly expand access to this technology in the U.S. and continue building on the momentum of one of the most active innovation periods in our history.” Built on the THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF Platform, which has extensive clinical validation and has treated over one million patients in the U.S., the DE STSF Platform brings pulse field capability to a catheter physicians know and trust.i The DE STSF platform is integrated with the CARTO ecosystem, including advanced mapping, imaging and PF Index guidance, helping physicians confidently deliver energy with precise contact force while supporting a predictable procedure and reproducible workflow. The dual energy capability gives physicians the versatility to use RF or PF energy based on patient anatomy and case complexity.i "Electrophysiologists need technologies that support different anatomies, substrates, workflows and treatment goals," said Dhanunjaya (DJ) Lakkireddy1, M.D., FHRS, MBA, Executive Medical Director, The Kansas City Heart Rhythm Institute. "The Dual Energy THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF Platform gives electrophysiologists the choice to use RF or PF energy based on the needs of each procedure. Having both capabilities integrated in the CARTO system can help us adapt our approach for more complex cases and plan procedures with greater confidence.” Following FDA approval, first U.S. procedures with the DE STSF Platform are expected to begin this summer as Johnson & Johnson initiates a phased commercial rollout. title: 6 Tangible Benefits of Account-Based Marketing (ABM)
summary: Learn the real benefits of account-based marketing. Align sales and marketing around high-value accounts to shorten cycles and increase deal sizes in 2026.
body_text: Book a Demo It wasn’t all that long ago that account-based marketing was a fairly obscure approach practiced only by enterprise sales teams targeting whales at other equally large companies. Today, account-based marketing (ABM) is a widely accepted practice and one that’s used not only by enterprise-level companies but also by mid-sized and small businesses alike. The thing with ABM is that it's not exactly something you can just tip a toe in like you can with something like digital advertising or outbound email. To be successful with account-based marketing, you need to go all in, which means you’ll need buy-in from every stakeholder on your leadership time. And, naturally, they’ll all ask the same thing before signing off: What are the benefits of account-based marketing? That’s the exact question we are going to answer in this guide, diving deep into the six important and tangible benefits of running an ABM playbook: 1. Aligns sales and marketing toward a common goal 2. Allows for a more focused use of resources 3. Creates a more customer-centric experience 4. Opens up a world of personalization 5. Can lead to shorter sales cycles 6. Sets you up for long-term customer relationships Account-based orchestration: Moving beyond ABM 1. Aligns sales and marketing toward a common goal The tension between sales and marketing teams is a thing of legend. It's kind of weird when you think about it. Both teams are, in the end, working toward the goal of closing more customers. There really shouldn’t be any turbulence here. But there often is, and that generally comes from a disconnection between the two teams that work in siloes and only on part of the problem. The sales and marketing problem Marketing works to attract new prospects to the company and capture leads. Sales then takes those leads and tries to convert them into customers. And that’s where the issue emerges. Sales blames marketing for poor quality leads. Marketing blames sales for not doing enough with the leads they’ve generated. But with an account-based marketing approach, this divide disappears. The ABM solution In ABM, you choose the accounts you go after. There is no “ lead generation ” in the traditional sense, as you define from the get-go who your target audience is going to be. Then, sales and marketing must collaborate to attract and close deals. There is no “marketing to sales handoff.” In the early stages of an ABM playbook, marketing might run personalized digital ads, while sales executes outreach via email and LinkedIn. Further down the sales funnel, the sales team might be engaging in demos and presentations while marketing supplements with additional educational email content. Members from each team work in parallel rather than in series, and they work together toward the same goal: closing target accounts. In fact, the alignment between sales and marketing that ABM brings is so strong that some organizations forgo the distinction altogether and merge the two departments into one GTM (go-to market) team: ( Image Source ) 2. Allows for a more focused use of resources One of the biggest problems with the traditional marketing model is that your use of resources is relatively unfocused. Sure, you have a defined target audience and ICPs (ideal customer profiles) that you’re going after. But the truth is that beyond that, your “targeting” is incredibly broad. Most of the people your ad campaigns, emails, and content marketing efforts get in front of aren’t in the market to buy right now, even if they fit your customer persona. Worse, you don’t even know if you’re getting in front of the decision-maker. Consider, for example, a prospect coming across a blog post you’ve written and then promoted on social media. That prospect signs up for a sales demo—great news, a warm lead . But after going through the whole presentation, your salesperson learns that they don’t actually have the authority to buy, and so the whole process needs to happen again with the decision-maker. Account-based marketing flips this on its head. Finding KDMs from day one You know who the key decision makers (KDMs) are in a given organization because you’ve used a tool like Warmly or Demandbase to pull account-level data and build a list of multiple stakeholders that might be involved in the deal. Then, your ABM efforts (be they personalized marketing outreach via LinkedIn InMail or a series of ads via your marketing automation platform) go out to those prospects specifically. All of this means that every dollar you spend on account-based marketing strategies is incredibly focused and spent only on the specific accounts that you want to start a conversation with. 3. Opens up a world of personalization One of the biggest benefits of ABM campaigns as a B2B marketing strategy is that you can run incredibly personalized campaigns. We’re not talking about using the prospect’s name in your email campaigns here. We’re talking: Using advanced marketing tools to deliver personalized ads across multiple platforms Target multiple stakeholders at the same time with a personalized and role-based email copy Using unconventional tactics like direct mail and personalized gifting to attract attention Here’s an extreme example to illustrate my point. When software design firm Intridea targeted Ogilvy as a key account in their account-based marketing campaign, they went as far as uncovering the daily commute of the decision-maker at their soon-to-be new customer and ran a custom billboard on the side of the street. ( Image Source ) 4. Creates a more customer-centric experience A well-executed ABM approach almost always leads to an enhanced customer experience when compared with a traditional marketing playbook. In the traditional marketing approach, every customer sees the same marketing programs and tactics. Sure, the content they see might be tailored to their current stage in the customer journey, but it's very rarely personalized to them specifically. But an ABM experience is all about that specific customer and is customized to individual accounts. As a prospect, all of the content you engage with is personalized to your company and even to you and your role. And when you speak to a member of the sales team, they aren’t giving you a blank slate templated pitch. They know who you are, and what success means for you in your role and at your company, and will deliver a tailored pitch that speaks exactly to those needs. It also blends seamlessly with an omnichannel approach, where you’re targeting multiple stakeholders in the buying committee with the right messaging at the right time via the right channel. That's critical because these days, there are more stakeholders than ever before , so the complexity of the deal has increased exponentially. You need solutions that give you signals as to who’s hot and warm in the committee and when they are thinking about you to know when and how to engage. This customer-centric approach ultimately leads to more effective campaigns that close faster. Speaking of which… 5. Can lead to shorter sales cycles Many advocates of an ABM process claim that it has helped them achieve a shorter sales cycle. ( Image Source ) This is going to be true in many cases, though we should be careful to say that there are a number of different variables here. The target audience you’re going after has a huge impact. Enterprise companies (who are more commonly the target of ABM campaigns) close slower than mid-sized organizations, as they often have large and elaborate buying committees. Your sales process itself also has some cards to play here, as do the specific account-based marketing activities you choose to engage in. On the whole, however, if you: Define your ideal customer profile correctly Build realistic account lists with accurate account data Supplement that with third-party buying intent data Execute well-timed and personalized ABM tactics that speak to ICP needs You should see shorter sales cycles from ABM compared to what you would otherwise see from a non-account-based approach. 6. Sets you up for long-term customer relationships Perhaps the most important of the six account-based marketing benefits discussed here is the fact that you’re building stronger relationships than you would be with a traditional motion. In a traditional marketing model, a given prospect isn’t considered a customer until you actually close the deal. Up until then, they’re just a lead. This inevitably frames all discussions up until contracting as sales conversations. An ABM motion, on the other hand, doesn’t really use the lead/customer division; they’re considered an account from the beginning. And because all of your marketing and sales activities are personalized to that specific account, you’re essentially using that as the starting point of your relationship-building efforts. This relationship is then transferred over to the customer success manager (or key accounts manager, depending on your chosen nomenclature). Their job is to nurture and grow the customer relationship rather than create it, which ultimately has a positive impact on customer retention rates. This distinction is why many account-based marketing teams choose to take a land-and-expand approach. The land and expand model The idea with land-and-expand is that your initial sales efforts aren’t about closing the biggest deal possible. They’re just about getting a foot in the door. You might sell your lowest-value product or most commonly used feature and narrow in on that to get a relationship established and a deal closed. Then, your CSM looks for opportunities to upsell to a more robust plan or cross-sell additional features as the relationship flourishes, the trust your client has for you grows, and they begin to see value from using your product. This is a fantastic tactic to add to your startup sales playbook, as it means you can get a door opened with just a single product or even an MVP and expand revenue from there. Account-based orchestration: Moving beyond ABM Account-based marketing clearly offers a number of important benefits. Most importantly, being a personalized approach, a successful ABM strategy ultimately leads to higher ROI and stronger customer relationships than a traditional marketing motion. While we’re fans of ABM programs in general—as compared to a more traditional alternative—we also believe there’s a better way, one which we call account-based orchestration . Account-based orchestration takes an ABM campaign to the next level and encompasses a more holistic approach that aligns both marketing and sales efforts. ( Image Source ) It incorporates various technologies (many of which are ABM tools), data-driven insights, and a heavy dose of AI and automation to execute at scale without needing a huge team. Read more: The Rise of Account-Based Orchestration in the Age of AI and Automation . We built Warmly to help small and medium-sized organizations access account-based orchestration on an SME budget, combining the best of advanced AI and best-in-class data with well-timed human intervention. With Warmly, you can: Deanonyomize site traffic to know exactly who is on your site and what content they’re engaging with Add identified prospects to an automated omnichannel outreach sequence on LinkedIn and email Capture immediate intent with an AI-led chatbot Get notifications via Slack when it is time for a sales rep to jump in and take over the chat What’s best about Warmly? You can get started for free, right now, without speaking to a sales rep or getting thrown into a sales funnel. Get set up with Warmly today, and start seeing ROI in minutes . Understanding these fundamentals helps B2B teams improve their sales and marketing effectiveness. Why is 6 Tangible Benefits of Account Based Marketing (ABM) important? This matters because it directly impacts pipeline generation and revenue. Teams that master these concepts see better results from their go-to-market efforts. How can I implement this? Start with the strategies outlined above. For B2B teams, combining these tactics with tools like Warmly—which identifies website visitors and automates engagement—can accelerate results. title: Biotech is Booming! Some Context and History Would Be Nice...So Here You Go

body_text: Since April 1st, 2025, the S&P Biotech Select Index (XBI) is up over 93% through 7/24/2026. Let's talk a little bit about what we have seen over the past few years. From 2016 to 2019, biotech certainly moved higher, but not significantly over a 4-year period. Then COVID happened, which was arguably the greatest cycle for biotech in its history (think zero % interest rates and a global pandemic where the entire world is funding, accelerating development, and recognizing the value biotech companies provide). You see that reflected in the XBI when it peaked in February 2021 at nearly $180. It was then a steady collapse as the sector unwound (for many reasons, including a lot of junk companies that never should have received funding to come public). It then just bounced around for several years before finally breaking out. We find it most interesting that the XBI is at all-time highs now, aside from the COVID period, when the backdrop is so much different. Interest rates are not zero. There is no global pandemic: Advancements in science continues to lead to new drugs in a variety of indications, from large oncology populations down to orphan diseases. Companies are getting better at targeting these populations, and while drug development is still fraught with failure, we see many great successes. M&A is alive and well. There have been numerous deals in 2026 already. It is well known that numerous large pharma blockbusters are coming off patent in the next 5+ years. These companies are all battling to enhance their pipelines to replaced future revenue pressure from generics. Sector quality is better. During COVID, money was pouring into biotech companies and management teams could advance their entire pipelines. This sounds great, but some assets were higher risk and likely shouldn’t have progressed. This took time to clear out. I’d argue small biotech pipeline quality is overall better today than the 2-3 years post COVID. Market-cap exposure for the index is worth discussing. XBI is currently ~80% invested in micro- and small-cap biotech stocks (generally under $10B in market cap). Mid-Cap ($10B–$50B market cap) represents about 15%. The XBI ETF entered 2025 close to its 3-year high before declining sharply early in the year, falling from roughly $90 to below $70 at the April lows — a peak-to-trough decline of over 20%. Biotech then rebounded strongly over the remainder of the year and has continued to shine in 2026.

title: Why SMR Cybersecurity Should Start Before the First Reactor Goes Online
summary: As SMR adoption grows, cybersecurity is becoming a critical design requirement. Explore best practices for securing future nuclear operations
body_text: AI data centers, net-zero commitments and industrial electrification are creating a new power problem. Demand is rising faster than many organizations can plan for, and interest in the small modular reactor market is growing as organizations look for future sources of reliable power. According to the International Energy Agency 1 , the pipeline of conditional agreements for data center operators to buy future power from small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear projects grew from 25 gigawatts (GW) at the end of 2024 to 45 GW, a scale roughly equivalent to dozens of large power plants. For the security community, this raises a practical question: Will cybersecurity be built into SMR plans early enough to protect the business case? The answer depends on decisions being made now. Architecture sets the foundation. Supplier requirements shape long-term risk. Access rules determine who can reach sensitive systems. Monitoring defines what security teams can see once a facility is operating. SMRs are not just smaller nuclear plants. They can rely on highly digital systems, lean operating teams and new ownership models. That makes cybersecurity a front-end planning issue, not a post-deployment fix. Why SMR Cybersecurity is Different Traditional nuclear facilities often have large on-site teams. They may have dedicated security operations resources, full compliance teams and deep internal nuclear expertise. The SMR business model relies on smaller sites, leaner teams and lower operating costs. If every site copies the staffing model of a large nuclear plant, the economics can quickly become difficult. Centralized or managed security may be part of what makes the SMR model work. Organizations planning for SMR deployment need to know: who owns cyber risk if a third party runs daily operations? Who sets security requirements? Who monitors the environment? Who is responsible when an incident involves a supplier, operator or remote support pathway? The answers matter because asset owners may still hold financial and regulatory risk, even when others manage daily operations. Why Cybersecurity Must Be Built Into SMR Design SMR cybersecurity should begin during front-end planning and engineering, before key decisions become difficult to change. That planning includes network architecture, how suppliers connect to systems, how patches are tested, how remote support is controlled and how monitoring data reaches security teams. Physical security should also be planned alongside cybersecurity, not treated as a separate track. Early planning should define the cybersecurity scope for front-end engineering design and set requirements for segmentation, continuous monitoring, endpoint visibility and secure access. Regulatory readiness also needs early attention. In the U.S., traditional nuclear cybersecurity programs reference Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Section 73.54, and Nuclear Energy Institute guidance such as NEI 08-09. Newer SMR approaches are moving toward more performance-based frameworks, including 10 CFR Part 53 and Draft Regulatory Guide 5075. For now, SMR security expectations are still evolving. Asset owners need a cybersecurity program that can be documented, tested and adapted as requirements mature. Secure Supply Chain Practices Reduce SMR Risk SMR supply chain security requires more than choosing trusted suppliers. Operators need to understand how systems will be built, updated and supported. These environments may depend on software, firmware, control systems, cybersecurity tools and long-term vendor support. That means supplier assurance has to continue after procurement. Operators should expect detailed software bills of materials. They should require clear patch and update processes. They should also look for vendor transparency around vulnerabilities and incidents. Factory Acceptance Testing can help validate systems before they arrive on site. Clear access rules can also reduce risk when vendors need to support or maintain equipment. SMR operators need confidence in how systems will be changed, tested and maintained over time. Remote Monitoring and Access Boundaries Remote support and centralized monitoring may become part of future SMR operating models, but access cannot be routine. Operators need to decide what can be monitored remotely and what requires strict on-site control. Security teams also need a way to detect abnormal activity, such as unexpected changes to system behavior. This requires a specialized OT SOC that understands the plant well enough to know the difference between a true cyber incident and a routine maintenance cycle or equipment failure. Vendor access should be approved, logged and reviewed and removable media should be tightly managed through secure, zero trust gatekeepers to detect walk-in threats from contractors before they enter the environment. The security benefit of a fully air-gapped environment may not be enough when asset owners need visibility across multiple SMR sites. This reality demands a deterministic approach to data transfer, extracting continuous operational telemetry for visibility without creating a bi-directional pathway that exposes the network. Hardware-based controls, such as embedded data diodes, can help by allowing data to move in one direction. Security teams gain the visibility they need, while critical systems remain tightly protected. SMR Operators Need Scalable Security Support Many future SMR operators may not have deep nuclear cybersecurity expertise in-house. Some may be entering the nuclear power sector for the first time. A scalable support model can help. This may include virtual CISO guidance, centralized OT security operations center services, and managed or co-managed cybersecurity support. A virtual CISO (vCISO) can be especially important for asset owners. Even when a third party operates the plant, the asset owner may still carry the risk. A vCISO can help define governance and track security performance across multiple SMR sites. This model can also support day-to-day needs such as monitoring, patching, antivirus, secure remote access, incident response and vulnerability management. Managed support does not replace operator accountability. Site knowledge, policies and procedures still matter. However, managed support services can help close gaps in expertise, governance and monitoring before they can become operational problems. How Honeywell Helps Organizations Prepare Honeywell supports organizations evaluating SMR deployment with OT cybersecurity expertise, network security monitoring, managed OT security services, patch management, antivirus support, and secure remote access. Organizations evaluating or building SMRs to meet power demands should reach out to Honeywell to assess their OT cybersecurity readiness. 1 International Energy Agency. “ Data centre electricity use surged in 2025, even with tightening bottlenecks driving a scramble for solutions .” Press release, April 16, 2026.

title: DeSoto Suburban: Chrysler’s Questionable Station-Wagon Alternative
summary: Mrs. Dozie Herbruck, wife of my high-school classmate Dave, mentioned at a recent reunion that her family had a three-row DeSoto sedan when she was a kid. I didn’t know such a car existed. Could she come up with a photo or two of the vehicle, and some childhood memories of it? “Your request for […]
body_text: Mrs. Dozie Herbruck, wife of my high-school classmate Dave, mentioned at a recent reunion that her family had a three-row DeSoto sedan when she was a kid. I didn’t know such a car existed. Could she come up with a photo or two of the vehicle, and some childhood memories of it? “Your request for a picture of our DeSoto sent me down memory lane,” she later responded via email. “We probably had it in the early ‘50s. I looked through all my mother’s slides and found pictures of every boat we owned, every fish caught, every beach visited but, alas, not one picture of the DeSoto. Apparently, my mother was as embarrassed by that car as my sisters and I were. “One sister remembers packing us all into it for a vacation to visit relatives in New Hampshire and driving over the scary Bear Mountain bridge. My brother thinks it was a Suburban sedan, semi-automatic with fluid drive. He remembers driving it (illegally, of course) and said he shifted it by pressing down on the accelerator. My other sister said she would hide when being dropped off at school because her friends all had station wagons and we had this ‘hearse.’” Her anecdotes might explain why DeSoto built so few Suburbans through its six model years. They might also explain why, as far as I know, no other Chrysler (or other) brand offered anything like the DeSoto. The story of the DeSoto Suburban turns out to be more complex, and interesting, than I anticipated. History Stellantis Named for the Spanish conquistador Hernando de Soto, the DeSoto Motor Car Company was founded in 1912 as a subsidiary of Zimmerman Manufacturing, a builder of horse buggies based in Auburn, Indiana. DeSoto was later acquired by the Auburn Automobile Company and in 1928 was reborn as the DeSoto Division of Chrysler Corporation, which planned for DeSoto to compete in the mid-price class with GM’s Pontiac and Oldsmobile, Ford’s Mercury, plus Hudson, Willys, and Studebaker, one step below Dodge and above Plymouth. Mecum A total of 81,065 DeSoto Sixes were built in 1929, a first-year U.S. production record that was not eclipsed until the 1960 Ford Falcon. Chrysler reversed the market positions of its mid-priced marques in 1933, re-ranking DeSoto above Dodge in hopes of boosting the latter brand’s sales. Unfortunately, DeSoto’s shorter-wheelbase versions of Chrysler’s streamlined 1934 Airflow proved unpopular. Unlike Chrysler, which continued to offer more traditional models in addition to the radical Airflow, DeSoto was hobbled by that Airflow design until new Airstream models arrived for 1935. Stretch Sedans With the resumption of civilian auto production following World War II, DeSoto’s 1942 models were reborn as 1946 models. For the 1947 model year, the long-wheelbase (139.5- vs. 121.5-inch) three-row Suburban sedan was added as DeSoto’s top-of-the-line, flagship offering. As the sales guide proclaimed, the Suburban “establish[ed] a new trend in motoring comfort”: “Even while easily seating nine persons, there is still more luggage space available than in a conventional sedan. Seating and carrying capacities are instantly interchangeable to suit varied requirements. Both first and second seats are full-sized and adjustable, the second having a 21-inch range, controlled by levers on both sides. Third, or auxiliary seat, is a substantial straight-across cushion with divided back and can be quickly flattened to become part of the floor or partially lowered to form a barrier between the luggage and the front compartments.” Eric Weiner Stellantis Stellantis Eric Weiner Stellantis The long adjustment travel of the second-row seat enabled it to be pushed far enough forward to create nearly seven feet of flat cargo floor, which was durable, laminated fir wood with chrome-plated skid strips. To accommodate heavy loads, the floor of the car’s chrome-railed rooftop luggage rack was made of sturdy plywood over a reinforced steel-on-steel roof panel. “It all adds up to a multi-purpose car of superb beauty, as modern as tomorrow,” the sales guide concluded. DeSoto’s Suburbans were initially powered by a 237-cubic-inch inline-six good for 109 hp (later increased to 112 hp, then to 116 hp with a displacement increase to 250 cubic inches for 1951) through a standard three-speed manual or optional Fluid Drive two-speed semi-automatic transmission. Eric Weiner Eric Weiner Eric Weiner Eric Weiner Eric Weiner The Suburban’s primary target was the upscale buyer with a large family who wanted the practicality of a station wagon with the styling, luxury and handling of a sedan. Offering exceptional interior and cargo roominess compared to typical competitors, plus all-steel construction in an era when station wagons typically had high-maintenance, rot-prone bodies made of wood, the Surburban also appealed to hotel and airport shuttle and taxi services. Some even became DeSoto limousines. Unusual for U.S. automakers, DeSoto offered no station wagon at the time and touted the Suburban as a better alternative. Eric Weiner While it earned some good press for innovative design, versatility and cargo and towing capabilities, the Suburban’s relatively high price of $2175 (about $33,000 in 2026 dollars) helped limit its sales to 3339 units in 1947 and total production to 7054 through ’48, according to Stellantis data (see chart below). The latter half of 1949 brought Chrysler Corporation’s first new postwar models and, for 1950, DeSoto’s first station wagon. Suburban production totaled just 2795 units. The new “Carry All” model accounted for all but 108 of them, with both second- and third-row seats folding flat to extend the cargo floor to the back of the front bench. An eight-passenger sedan (the sales guide called it the “Seven-Passenger”), with foldable, “adult-size” jump seats between the front and rear benches, accounted for another 186 units. The 1950 model year saw 4498 DeSoto Suburban Sedans and 825 Eight-Passenger Sedans built, while Korean-War years 1951–52 added 2192 Suburbans and 768 Eight-Passenger Sedans. In 1953 and 1954, Stellantis reports that 338 and 307, respectively, of the latter were built, but no Suburbans. Given the ravages of rust and the relative unpopularity of these cars (Herbruck’s father donated the car to the Red Cross when the family “finally got a real car,” in her words), very few remain today as collector pieces. The End Mecum In 1952, DeSoto added a series of Firedome models with 276-cubic-inch V-8 Hemi engines . For ’53, the automaker dropped its long-running Deluxe and Custom trim names and designated its six-cylinder cars “ Powermaster s.” For 1955, all Chrysler Corp. models were redesigned with Virgil Exner’s “Forward Look,” and DeSotos, with impressively soaring tailfins and triple taillamps, sold in record numbers. A 1956 DeSoto even served as the Indianapolis 500 pace car. The ‘57s also did well, but the 1958 economic downturn hurt sales of all mid-priced cars, and DeSoto sales were down 60% versus 1957, marking their worst year since 1938. After sales continued to plunge through 1959 and 1960, Chrysler canceled its DeSoto marque after the 1961 model year. In all, more than two million passenger cars and trucks bore the DeSoto (aka De Soto) brand in North American markets, of which more than 16,000 were long-wheelbase Suburbans. While Chevrolet’s Suburban truck-based wagons have been built and successfully sold since 1935, DeSoto’s 1947–52 Suburban Sedans were an early precursor to today’s hugely popular car-based SUVs and crossovers.
