title: Hyper-V vs. VMware vs. Azure Local (and Others): 2026 Comparison and Migration Guide
summary: Compare Nutanix AHV and VMware ESXi on architecture, licensing, management, and migration to choose the right hypervisor for your data center.
body_text: Summary The 2026 virtualization landscape is shifting rapidly. This guide compares Hyper-V, VMware, Azure Local, and other key platforms to help you choose the right virtualization strategy for your organization. For years, comparing Hyper-V vs. VMware was a predictable debate over licensing fine print and minor feature gaps. But in 2026, the landscape has fundamentally shifted. Following Broadcom’s licensing restructuring , some organizations face astronomical renewal costs, forcing a massive, high-stakes migration wave. Whether you’re executing a VMware-to-Hyper-V migration, exploring Microsoft’s rebranded hybrid powerhouse Azure Local (formerly Azure Stack HCI), or looking at open source alternatives, the decision is no longer just “which hypervisor is better.” The real 2026 decision set requires weighing post-Broadcom cost pressures against modern hybrid cloud architecture. This guide breaks down your best paths forward, digging into the nuances of Azure Local combinations and also comparing the legacy giants with today’s other, newer alternatives: Proxmox , Nutanix , and XCP-ng . First, let’s look at how what may be the biggest news event in virtualization history has changed things. Figure 1: The 2026 Virtualization Crossroads — VMware by Broadcom vs. Hyper-V vs. Azure Local. Overview of VMware by Broadcom Pioneering virtualization since 1998, VMware, officially rebranded as VMware by Broadcom, remains the gold standard for enterprise virtualization. Its vSphere platform has evolved into one of the most reliable, feature-rich private cloud environments available. Like Hyper-V, ESXi (VMware’s core hypervisor) is a Type 1 bare metal hypervisor renowned for its high performance, robust security, and deep resource management capabilities. Historically, the VMware ecosystem was highly modular, allowing organizations to purchase standalone licenses for vSphere, vSAN (storage), and NSX (networking) as needed. The 2026 VMware subscription bundles: VCF vs. VVF Under Broadcom’s restructured model, standalone product licensing is gone. Virtually all deployments have been consolidated into two primary per-core subscription packages: VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF): This is Broadcom’s flagship, enterprise-grade private cloud suite. It’s a complete, tightly integrated software-defined data center (SDDC) stack that bundles vSphere (compute), vSAN (storage), NSX (networking), and the Aria Suite (advanced management and automation). VCF is built for large-scale and rapid hybrid-cloud deployments. VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF): Positioned as the mid-market and standard enterprise offering, VVF focuses primarily on core compute virtualization. It packages vSphere, vSphere Kubernetes Service (formerly Tanzu Kubernetes Grid), and basic operations management, along with a limited, trial-sized capacity of vSAN storage (typically capped per core). (Note: Bare-bones vSphere Standard is still offered for basic workloads, but it lacks the advanced storage and management capabilities of the Foundation suites). The Broadcom effect: What changed with VMware licensing? If your organization is approaching a virtualization renewal, you’re likely facing a drastically different commercial reality. Since Broadcom completed its acquisition of VMware, it has introduced major licensing changes that have left many IT teams facing higher costs and increased pressure to evaluate alternatives. The disruption comes down to four fundamental shifts: 1. The end of perpetual licenses The era of buying a VMware license once and running it indefinitely with optional Support and Subscription (SnS) is over. Broadcom has discontinued perpetual licensing. Once your current SnS contract expires, you must either transition to a recurring subscription or run unsupported without security patches, upgrades, or technical assistance. 2. Mandatory, high-cost ‘all-or-nothing’ bundles To simplify its catalog and drive revenue, Broadcom consolidated dozens of granular, standalone products into rigid subscription bundles. Granular options are gone. If you want advanced features, you need VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). VCF forces you to pay for the “full stack,” including compute (vSphere), storage (vSAN), networking (NSX), and management (Aria), regardless of whether you actually use or need those individual components. 3. Core licensing shifts and minimums Licensing has shifted from a per-CPU socket model to a per-core subscription model. This transition is accompanied by costly constraints: The 16-core socket minimum: Every physical CPU socket requires a minimum of 16 licensed cores. The 72-core contract minimum: Broadcom implemented a strict minimum purchase threshold of 72 cores per contract. Small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) or edge deployments with low-core physical servers often see their licensing requirements (and costs) increase significantly for the exact same physical hardware. Late renewal surcharges: Missing your contract anniversary date triggers a 20% surcharge on your first-year subscription cost with no grace period. 4. Partner ecosystem disruption Broadcom ended VMware’s legacy partner programs, eliminating thousands of smaller, regional distributors and resellers to focus strictly on top-tier “Pinnacle” and “Premier” partners. For mid-market businesses, this means the trusted local IT providers who managed their VMware environments for years may no longer have direct access to deal registration or specialized discounts, driving up procurement friction and costs. The bottom line With average renewal costs increasing anywhere from 2X to 12X , the Broadcom effect has transformed virtualization from a routine infrastructure utility into an active financial liability. This pressure is the primary driver behind the wave of migrations toward Hyper-V and the adoption of modern hybrid alternatives like Azure Local, which we’ll get into now. Overview of Hyper-V Microsoft introduced Hyper-V in 2008 as a native hypervisor, seamlessly integrated into Windows Server. Since then, it has been a core component of every Windows Server release, including Windows Server 2025, as well as desktop Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions. As a Type 1 hypervisor , Hyper-V runs directly on the bare metal hardware rather than as an application inside an operating system. This architecture ensures high-speed performance, low overhead, and efficient physical resource allocation. The licensing advantage: ‘Included’ virtualization One of Hyper-V’s biggest advantages in 2026 is its licensing model. Unlike VMware’s post-Broadcom per-core subscription bundles, Hyper-V licensing is built directly into Windows Server: Windows Server Standard Edition includes virtualization rights for up to two VMs per licensed host. Windows Server Datacenter Edition grants unlimited VM rights on licensed host hardware. If your organization already licenses Windows Server for its workloads, Hyper-V is essentially “free” virtualization, completely bypassing separate hypervisor licensing fees. Additionally, Microsoft’s flexible licensing models now include pay-as-you-go subscription licensing via Azure Arc, allowing organizations to pay for Windows Server on a flexible, per-core monthly basis without needing upfront perpetual licenses. Key features of Hyper-V To compete in a highly demanding market, Hyper-V features deep native integration with the Microsoft ecosystem, robust clustering, and cloud-management capabilities: Nested virtualization: Enables you to run virtual machines inside other virtual machines. This is a critical feature for DevOps pipelines, software testing, and mimicking multi-node configurations on a single physical host. Dynamic memory: Intelligently reclaims and reallocates RAM across running VMs in real time based on active workload demands, preventing wasted memory overhead. Live migration: Allows you to move running VMs between physical clustering hosts with zero downtime or service interruption, ensuring seamless hardware maintenance. Azure Arc integration: Windows Server and Hyper-V feature deep native integration with Azure Arc , Microsoft’s platform for managing resources that don’t live in Azure as if they do. By onboarding your Hyper-V hosts to Azure Arc, you can manage on-premises VMs directly from the Azure Portal. This unlocks cloud-native capabilities on premises—including centralized patch management, Azure Monitor, policy governance, and even no-cost Hotpatching (which allows you to apply security patches to Windows Server 2025 VMs in memory without rebooting). Overview of Azure Local If Windows Server Hyper-V is Microsoft’s traditional approach to virtualization, Azure Local is its modern, cloud-native successor. Rebranded from Azure Stack HCI, Azure Local is a purpose-built, hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) operating system designed to run virtual machines, containerized applications, and cloud services directly on your physical on-premises hardware. Under the hood, Azure Local still utilizes the Hyper-V hypervisor engine and Storage Spaces Direct (S2D). However, it strips away traditional Windows Server roles (like Active Directory, print servers, or DNS) to function as a lean, high-performance hybrid virtualization host. Key features of Azure Local Native Azure Arc control plane: Unlike standard hypervisors managed via local desktop apps, Azure Local is cloud native. It installs with an integrated Azure Arc resource bridge, turning your physical local servers into an extension of the public cloud. You can provision, resize, patch, and delete on-premises VMs directly through the Azure Portal web browser, or by using cloud-standard tools like Bicep, Terraform, and the Azure CLI. Hyperconverged (and disaggregated) storage: Azure Local naturally leverages local server NVMe and SSD storage to create a highly resilient, ultra-fast software-defined storage pool. However, to directly compete with premium SAN architectures, it also supports disaggregated SAN deployments—allowing organizations to attach enterprise Storage Area Networks and scale their compute nodes independently past traditional 16-node limits. Integrated Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS): Container management is baked into the platform. You can run traditional monolithic VMs side by side with localized AKS container clusters managed seamlessly under one cloud roof. Hardware-accelerated AI workloads: Azure Local features mature support for GPU acceleration (via GPU partitioning or Discrete Device Assignment), allowing local virtual machines to leverage enterprise hardware like NVIDIA L-series and Blackwell GPUs for localized AI models and heavy graphic processing. Sovereign and disconnected operations: For environments with strict data privacy laws or flaky internet, Azure Local features a Sovereign Private Cloud stack. It can run in completely “disconnected” or air-gapped modes—keeping your local mission-critical workloads, compliance policies, and even Microsoft 365 Local services running autonomously without constant cloud connectivity. The Azure Local consumption model Azure Local changes how virtualization is bought. Rather than purchasing permanent software licenses upfront, it operates on an operating expense ( OPEX ) utility model billed directly to your monthly Azure account, and pricing for external storage is still in flux. The hybrid catch: While the host operating system is subscription-billed, guest operating system licenses (like Windows Server or Red Hat Linux running inside the VMs) are managed separately. If you already own Windows Server Datacenter licenses with Software Assurance, you can apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to waive the guest VM licensing fees, making it a highly cost-effective destination for migrating off VMware. Comparing Hyper-V, VMware, and Azure Local Integration and compatibility In 2026, compatibility is less about whether a hypervisor can run an operating system (all three handle Windows and Linux flawlessly) and more about cloud integration, containerization, and lock-in avoidance. Hyper-V (Windows Server): The traditional Microsoft engine OS support: Hyper-V has run enterprise Linux workloads (like Red Hat, Ubuntu, and Rocky Linux) with native, high-performance integration services baked directly into the Linux kernel for years. Cloud strategy: Hyper-V is highly optimized for organizations leveraging Azure Arc. If you want a consistent operating experience between your physical servers and the public cloud, Microsoft provides a seamless, unified control plane. Containerization: To run Kubernetes , standard Hyper-V relies on you manually provisioning and managing your own Linux virtual machines to act as container hosts, or using third-party distributions. Azure Local: The cloud-native hybrid platform OS support: Because it shares the core Hyper-V hypervisor, it runs Windows and Linux workloads with bare metal efficiency. However, it completely strips away traditional Windows Server roles to function purely as an optimized cloud-host OS. Cloud strategy: Azure Local is an extension of the cloud. It features native, out-of-the-box infrastructure projection via Azure Arc. You manage, configure, and scale your on-premises hardware directly from a web browser inside the Azure Portal using Azure Resource Manager (ARM). Containerization: It features native, turn-key integration for AKS on premises. There’s no control-plane licensing premium for AKS on Azure Local; container clusters cost only the underlying host cores you’re already paying for. VMware by Broadcom: The multi-cloud standard OS support: VMware’s guest OS support remains the broadest in the industry, maintaining highly mature templates for legacy operating systems, specialized Linux distributions, and even macOS (under specific hardware licensing). Cloud strategy: Through VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), Broadcom offers deep integration with AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. However, running VMware software on these public clouds now requires bringing your own expensive Broadcom subscription licenses (BYOL), making multi-cloud architectures significantly more expensive than they were a few years ago. Containerization: Container management is natively integrated into the virtualization layer via the vSphere Kubernetes Service, allowing IT operators to spin up and manage Kubernetes clusters side by side with traditional VMs using the familiar vCenter console. 2026 takeaway: If you want a tight, cost-effective on-premises-to-Azure pipeline, Microsoft is the clear winner. If you run a highly diverse, multi-cloud environment with legacy operating systems and have the budget to sustain it, VMware remains highly flexible. Security features All three platforms deliver enterprise-grade security, but their focus splits between cloud-backed governance, rigid hardware baselines, and full-stack software isolation. Hyper-V security: Active local protection Hyper-V uses virtual Trusted Platform Modules (vTPMs) to support Secure Boot and BitLocker encryption inside virtual machines, protecting them from virtual disk theft. While Shielded VMs (which encrypt VM data to protect it from compromised host administrators) are still supported, Microsoft has largely transitioned its development focus toward Azure Confidential Computing and hardware-enforced enclave security. Standard Hyper-V hosts can be hooked into Microsoft Defender for Endpoint manually or via basic Arc connection to stream hypervisor and guest OS security telemetry. Azure Local security: Zero-trust by default Azure Local is a “secure-by-default” operating system, shipping with over 300 security settings and explicit application control baselines strictly enabled right from the deployment phase. Built-in drift protection mechanisms continuously monitor your hardware, firmware, and hypervisor configurations. If a local administrator alters a security baseline, the platform flags it inside the Azure Portal and can automatically remediate the drift. Native, deep agent integration means advanced threat defense, automated vulnerability scanning, and SIEM data forwarding are built directly into the cluster infrastructure layer. VMware security: Cryptographic attestation and Carbon Black vSphere Trust Authority provides cryptographic attestation for the entire cluster, ensuring that only trusted hardware, firmware, and hypervisors can run sensitive workloads. With the deprecation of legacy tools like AppDefense, VMware has deeply integrated Carbon Black Workload directly into vSphere. It monitors VM behavior, detects anomalous processes, and can trigger network isolation via NSX to stop lateral threats in real time. VM-level encryption, core dump encryption, and secure boot are robustly supported, but securing the entire virtualized network fabric relies heavily on having the NSX security features bundled into the premium VCF tier. Architectural and feature comparison matrix The virtualization decision in 2026 isn’t just a comparison of raw hypervisor engines; it’s a choice between three distinct operational models. The breakdown below details how traditional Windows Server Hyper-V, Azure Local, and VMware by Broadcom stack up across core architectural features. Feature Hyper-V (Windows Server) Azure Local VMware by Broadcom (VVF/VCF) Hypervisor Type Type 1 (bare metal) Type 1 (optimized Hyper-V kernel) Type 1 (ESXi) Operational Model Traditional, isolated on-premises data center Cloud-managed, hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) Dedicated private cloud software stack Primary Management Tool Windows Admin Center, Hyper-V Manager, Failover Cluster Manager Azure Portal (ARM/Bicep), with Windows Admin Center for node diagnostics vCenter Server (natively bundled) Scale Limits Up to 64 nodes per cluster Up to 16 nodes per cluster Up to 64 nodes (vSAN) or 96 nodes (SAN) Live Workload Mobility Live migration (included, manual or cluster-based orchestration) Live migration (orchestrated natively via Azure Arc and local failover) vMotion (highly advanced, automated cross-cluster/vCenter mobility) Storage Integration Flexible: Supports traditional external SAN/NAS or Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) Native HCI via S2D (pools local NVMe/SSD) or specialized disaggregated SAN arrays vSAN (software-defined storage, kernel-integrated but requires high-tier bundling) Nested Virtualization Yes Yes Yes Resource Allocation Dynamic memory, static weights Dynamic memory, optimized host balancing Advanced DRS (continuous, automated vMotion load balancing) High Availability (HA) Failover clustering (configured manually with quorum/witness) Automated cloud-enforced HA (extends cluster logic via Azure policies) Policy-driven HA (advanced VM restart priorities, admission control) Disaster Recovery Hyper-V Replica, Azure Site Recovery Azure Site Recovery (cloud-native integration), stretch clusters Live Site Recovery (formerly SRM), vSphere Replication Native Kubernetes No (requires manual VM provisioning and standalone cluster setup) Yes (built-in AKS) with zero control-plane licensing fees Yes (vSphere Kubernetes Service) baked into the base foundation packages Support and community The support experience for these platforms has undergone a divergence, driven primarily by corporate restructuring and cloud alignment. Hyper-V support: The traditional IT ecosystem Microsoft offers a highly accessible support system. Because Hyper-V is built into Windows Server, standard Microsoft Unified Support covers your virtualization stack. The community is massive, highly collaborative, and deeply integrated with the broader Windows and Azure ecosystems. Troubleshooting resources, forums, and scripts are abundant and freely accessible to IT professionals of all levels. Azure Local support: Unified cloud escalation Support for Azure Local bypasses traditional Windows Server channels. Because it’s an active Azure service, technical support tickets are opened directly through the Azure Help + Support portal. Microsoft cloud engineers handle the host OS, Azure Arc control plane, and Azure-provided extensions collectively. While growing rapidly due to the post-Broadcom migration wave, the Azure Local community is highly cloud-centric, drawing heavily from enterprise DevOps, hybrid-cloud architects, and specialized hardware OEM implementation teams. VMware by Broadcom: Dedicated but enterprise-segmented Broadcom has heavily restructured VMware’s support delivery. Under the new model, support is bundled with the VCF and VVF subscriptions. Because Broadcom terminated the vast majority of smaller, regional VMware reseller partnerships to focus on top-tier enterprise accounts, mid-market customers often experience longer wait times and must navigate direct Broadcom support portals without the help of a local, dedicated partner. The VMware user community (VMUG) remains one of the most passionate and highly skilled technical communities in IT history. However, the pool of certified VMware professionals is experiencing shifts as many engineers actively cross-train in Hyper-V, Azure, and open source alternatives like Proxmox. Pricing Virtualization costs are no longer apples-to-apples. The final choice often comes down to capital expenditures (CAPEX) versus operational, utility-billed cloud expenses (OPEX). Here is approximate pricing. Pricing Component Hyper-V (Windows Server 2025) Azure Local (HCI) VMware by Broadcom (VVF/VCF) Billing Model Traditional license + software assurance (CAPEX) Monthly cloud subscription billed to Azure (OPEX) Annual/multi-year subscription contract (OPEX/CAPEX) Metrics Per physical core (minimum 16 cores/server) Per physical host core Per physical core (minimum 16 cores/CPU) Base Host Pricing Included with Windows Server ($0 extra if OS is licensed) $10/core/month (hyperconverged S2D) $20.10/core/month (disaggregated SAN) vSphere Foundation (VVF): ~$35–$50/core/year Cloud Foundation (VCF): ~$350+/core/year (Est. enterprise list) Guest VM Rights Standard: Up to 2 Windows VMs Datacenter: Unlimited Windows VMs Optional add-on: $23.30/core/month for unlimited Windows Server guests N/A (guest OS licenses must be purchased entirely separately via Microsoft) The “Cloud Trap”/Discounts No active cloud connection required. Traditional volume discounts apply Azure Hybrid Benefit (AHB): If you own Windows Server Datacenter with SA, host and guest fees can drop to $0/month Eliminates all perpetual assets. Rigid SKU bundling forces payment for unused features (vSAN/NSX) The core decision set in 2026 1. The legacy status quo: VMware by Broadcom The deal: You stay on ESXi/vSphere. You get deep, mature virtualization features (like DRS) and high performance, but you must absorb the price increases of Broadcom’s all-or-nothing software bundles (VCF/VVF). The fit: Highly complex environments with massive budgets that are deeply integrated into VMware’s automation ecosystem. 2. The traditional on-premises alternative: Windows Server Hyper-V The deal: You buy traditional Windows Server licenses (Standard or Datacenter) and turn on the Hyper-V role. You manage it locally via Hyper-V Manager, Failover Cluster Manager, or SCVMM. You plug it into your existing traditional SAN. The fit: Organizations that want a traditional capital expense (CAPEX) model, want to keep their existing non-HCI storage hardware, and want a low-cost, predictable alternative to Broadcom with zero cloud requirements. 3. The cloud-connected HCI alternative: Azure Local The deal: You deploy a dedicated hyperconverged infrastructure platform on validated partner hardware. Instead of buying Windows Server software licenses, you pay a monthly per-core subscription fee billed straight to your Azure portal ($10/physical core/month). You manage your on-premises virtual machines directly from the cloud using Azure Arc. The fit: Organizations doing a full hardware refresh, those looking to replace traditional SANs with modern hyperconverged storage (Storage Spaces Direct), and teams that want an operational model that acts exactly like Microsoft Azure but runs physically inside their own server room. Other options: Proxmox, Nutanix, and XCP-ng While the Microsoft stack captures a massive chunk of displaced VMware workloads, it isn’t the only destination. A growing number of enterprises are opting for open source flexibility or dedicated hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) alternatives to regain financial control. 1. Proxmox VE: The open source mid-market hero Proxmox Virtual Environment (VE) has graduated from homelabs to a legitimate enterprise replacement for VMware vSphere. Based on Debian Linux, it integrates the high-performance KVM hypervisor and lightweight LXC containers into a single, unified platform. The Proxmox Datacenter Manager (PDM): Released in late 2025, PDM functions as Proxmox’s answer to vCenter. It provides a clean, single pane of glass to manage multi-cluster environments across separate data centers. The financial appeal: Proxmox is entirely open source and free to download. However, production environments rely on the Proxmox Enterprise Subscription, which provides access to heavily tested stable repositories and vendor technical support. Crucially, it is billed per physical CPU socket, bypassing Broadcom’s punitive per-core minimums. Storage flexibility: It features native, out-of-the-box support for high-performance file systems like ZFS and integrated Ceph software-defined storage, mimicking many core capabilities of VMware vSAN. The catch: While its built-in ESXi import wizard makes migration straightforward, Proxmox demands strong in-house Linux scripting expertise. If your team relies heavily on turnkey enterprise ecosystems or extensive third-party automation tools, you’ll face an adaptation learning curve. When it comes to the backup ecosystem, unlike other hypervisors that force you into expensive third-party tools, the Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) offers enterprise-grade deduplication, encryption, and incremental backups natively integrated into the cluster layer. 2. Nutanix (AHV): The premium enterprise powerhouse If Proxmox is the choice for cost-conscious mid-market setups, Nutanix is the logical destination for massive, complex enterprise environments that want to move away from Broadcom but keep premier corporate backing. Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure (NCI) and AHV: Nutanix operates on its own Acropolis Hypervisor (AHV), built on a highly customized KVM foundation. It represents an operational model shift away from VMware’s complex, distributed dependency tree toward localized cluster authority—meaning individual nodes and clusters maintain complete operational resilience even if upstream management planes fail. Predictable licensing: While still a premium-tier enterprise software product, Nutanix has capitalized heavily on Broadcom migrations by offering modular, capacity-based licensing. You license what your infrastructure footprint actually uses rather than being penalized by rigid transistor or physical core minimums. Nutanix Move: To facilitate the migration wave, the platform includes the Nutanix Move toolkit, which automates the agentless cross-platform migration of VMs from ESXi to AHV with negligible cutover downtime. The catch: Nutanix is not cheap. While it undercuts post-acquisition VMware costs and offers much better stability, it requires a significant capital commitment and a potential redesign of deep network microsegmentation topologies if you previously relied heavily on VMware NSX. 3. XCP-ng: The Xen ecosystem drop-in XCP-ng (Xen Cloud Platform – next generation) is a fully open source, bare metal Type 1 hypervisor based directly on the classic XenServer architecture. Xen Orchestra (XO): The platform is managed via Xen Orchestra, a comprehensive web administration appliance. XO includes a powerful V2V (VMware-to-Vates) migration engine that allows for streaming, agentless warm migration of live virtual machines directly out of VMware environments into XCP-ng. Architectural progress: The platform has matured dramatically, with the modern QCOW2 storage format hitting general availability (GA), introducing high-performance snapshots, fast online coalescing, and built-in virtual disk compression. The appeal: XCP-ng is a true drop-in architectural replacement for teams that love the classic structural partitioning of traditional hypervisors but want an active, open source development path supported by a reliable corporate backing entity (Vates) providing SLA-driven production support. 2026 alternatives decision matrix To wrap up your strategic review, use this baseline breakdown to filter your options outside the Microsoft ecosystem: Platform Best Suited For Key Strength Main Tradeoff Proxmox VE SMBs, mid-market enterprises, and heavy dev/test environments Cost disruptive per-socket pricing, native LXC container options Demands a strong hands-on culture and solid Linux admin skills Nutanix (AHV) Large, regulated enterprises requiring premium 24X7 vendor backing Elite localized cluster resilience, seamless automated migration via Move High initial investment; a premium enterprise software tool XCP-ng Teams looking for an open-source, classic hypervisor layout Excellent Xen Orchestra management plane and robust warm V2V migration Smaller third-party ecosystem compared to KVM or Hyper-V variants Understand the True Cost of Your Virtualization Choice Broadcom’s licensing restructuring has dramatically shifted the virtualization landscape. Explore how these changes impact your infrastructure costs and why forward-thinking teams are evaluating alternative platforms. Learn About Broadcom Changes

title: Complete raises $4M seed funding to turn candidate offers and employee compensation into a strategic advantage
summary: It’s a big day for us at Complete! We’ve raised $4M in seed funding led by Accel, with support from Y Combinator. Angel investors include executives from Calm, Opendoor and Stripe. This news comes on the heels of our completion of Y Combinator earlier this year.
body_text: It’s a big day for us at Complete! We’ve raised $4M in seed funding led by Accel, with support from Y Combinator. Angel investors include executives from Calm, Opendoor and Stripe. This news comes on the heels of our completion of Y Combinator earlier this year. We thought it’d be a great opportunity for us to share more about what we’re building at Complete , technology that turns employee compensation into a strategic advantage. Many companies see their compensation plans as an afterthought. We want to help businesses get compensation right from the beginning, because it plays a crucial role in how both candidates and employees develop trust with their employer. Meanwhile, historically, there’s been very little accountability around compensation – people don’t know what questions to ask or who’s the right person to discuss it with. That’s where we come in. At Complete, we believe leading with transparency across the organization is core to a company’s DNA. We want founders, executives, candidates, and employees to understand why and how compensation decisions are made, starting with their compensation philosophy. Our technology starts by allowing companies to create compensation philosophies that align with their business goals and are then implemented company-wide, so that there’s no guesswork involved and teams can be assured they’re offering fair and equitable compensation plans. We integrate across the people lifecycle - starting with the candidates through their Applicant Tracking System down to the employee records through their HRIS. From there, we’ve created an unmatched offer experience that is interactive, engaging, and educational. We help candidates fully comprehend the company’s compensation philosophy before getting a deep view of every aspect of their offer, including cash, equity, bonuses, and benefits. Features include calculators and sliders, so that candidates also understand their long term earning potential. This interactivity and visibility is what we have recently extended to employees as well, so they have a source of truth to their evolving compensation plans. When people are able to comprehend the full value of an offer, even when it comes to equity and benefits that are complex or difficult to grasp, we’ve found applicants are 30% more likely to accept their offer when companies are transparent and forthcoming about how they approach company building and compensation. This is massive in the talent market that has seen record high vacant roles and high turnover from employees. Today we work with dozens of companies, including growth-stage companies like Convex and TrueNorth, as well as established companies like Vercel and DataStax. We’ve evaluated over 5,000 salaries and employee records to help our customers retain their top talent, as well as hold their teams accountable to their own best practices. This capital will allow us to make key strategic hires across product and design, so we can expand our onboarding platform to be even more powerful. “Competition for exceptional talent is fierce, and in today’s changing market, candidates and employees struggle to make sense of what their total equity package might be worth now and in the future,” said Amy Saper, Partner, Accel. “Complete enables companies to use compensation as a critical tool to help close and retain top talent. Their platform is uniquely focused on helping startups set the right compensation foundation from the beginning, while providing a suite of tools that enable talent, finance, and people teams to collaborate around the candidate and employee experience as their organizations scale.” We’re in the midst of a rebalancing - between the Great Renegotiation, a changing economic landscape and post-covid re-evaluation. People are deeply evaluating roles for the right fit considering location, company size, stage and more. COVID and inflation may have been symptoms, but they are not the cause; the American work culture has been in need of major changes for decades. Complete is here to help build out a new structure, bringing a culture of transparency around compensation practices and philosophy, both internally and externally. Throughout our careers at companies like Google, Uber, Lyft and Opendoor, we saw just how tough hiring can be – even for a big well known brand – and how confusion over compensation was often at the core of it. The hours we spent chatting through offers and promotions with team members are what we're channeling in an end-to-end product experience for high growth companies so winning isn't guesswork (or luck) anymore. We’re excited to help a new generation of companies and employees match with one another by creating deeper connection and understanding. If you’d like to get in touch or are interested in learning more about how our product can work for your business, request a demo .

title: Customers wanted full-game injury protection. FanDuel launched Bet Protect+
body_text: What this tells you about Flutter's product approach While Bet Protect+ is a product of FanDuel, Flutter's leading US sportsbook, it further demonstrates how Flutter brands prioritize the customer experience, with similar offerings available in other sports in other key sports betting markets. Across its global portfolio – which includes Paddy Power and Betfair in the UK and Ireland, Sisal in Italy, and Sportsbet in Australia – Flutter has consistently invested in proprietary product features that create differentiation through personalized offers and tailored generosity, rather than purely promotional spend. In the U.S., FanDuel has stated it will not profit from Bet Protect+ directly. The 3% premium covers the cost of providing the protection, not margin. By making the feature opt-in and self-funded, FanDuel avoids a trade-off common across the industry: funding promotional offers through less competitive odds or reduced generosity elsewhere on the platform. Customer research drove the design. More than half of surveyed users chose paid full-game protection over free partial coverage, with the preference strongest among experienced bettors who evaluate wagers in terms of expected value. The product was built around what customers wanted, not what was cheapest to offer. **The feature is available in most US states where FanDuel operates. Customers in Massachusetts, Connecticut, North Carolina, Tennessee, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey currently retain free first-quarter injury coverage with bonus bet refunds.

Base10-backed Throxy challenges AI sales giants with pay-per-meeting model - Throxy
summary: A London-based startup is betting that artificial intelligence has created more problems than solutions in sales automation, raising $6.2 million to target some of the economy's most lucrative but hard-to-reach industries with a decidedly human-first approach. Read the original article on Venturebeat here.
body_text: Read the original article on Venturebeat here A London-based startup is betting that artificial intelligence has created more problems than solutions in sales automation, raising $6.2 million to target some of the economy's most lucrative but hard-to-reach industries with a decidedly human-first approach. Throxy , which provides fully managed outbound sales services for companies selling into traditional sectors like manufacturing, logistics and medical equipment, closed the seed round led by Base10 Partners with participation from Y Combinator . The funding comes as the three-year-old company claims to have reached $1.5 million in annual recurring revenue with just three employees — a ratio that would make even Silicon Valley's most efficient startups envious. The company's emergence highlights a growing backlash against the proliferation of AI-powered sales tools that promise automation but often deliver diminishing returns . While venture capitalists have poured billions into AI sales development representatives (SDRs) and automated outreach platforms, Throxy's founders argue these tools have fundamentally missed their mark. "AI-generated messaging does not resonate a lot with the market, and it's not very effective," said Pablo Jiménez de Parga Ramos, Throxy's co-founder, in an exclusive interview with VentureBeat. "We barely use AI there. We think the best messages, at least as in today, are generated by humans." Why manufacturers and logistics firms can't find good sales leads The challenge Throxy aims to solve stems from a fundamental mismatch between modern sales technology and traditional industries that form the backbone of the global economy. Companies selling software or services to manufacturers, distributors, healthcare providers and logistics firms struggle to find and reach decision makers who often have minimal digital footprints. "One of the biggest issues for sales teams is people don't have enough pipeline," Jiménez de Parga explained. Having worked at three business-to-business software companies from seed stage to Series D, he witnessed the same problem repeatedly: sales teams spending up to 70% of their time on prospecting rather than closing deals. The root issue is data scarcity. While LinkedIn boasts 1.1 billion users globally, Throxy has built a database of over 4 billion contacts by mining public company registries, government databases and other sources that traditional sales tools ignore. In the United Kingdom alone, Companies House contains information on 6 million businesses, most of which never appear in conventional lead generation platforms. "Every single country has company registers," Jiménez de Parga noted. "Every single company also has directors, and all that information is publicly available and you can download it. Yet at my previous companies, we were not using that." This data advantage becomes particularly valuable in traditional industries where employee tenure spans decades rather than years. "In traditional spaces, people stay — if you find information about a person in 2011, they're probably still there," he said. How Throxy beats AI tools by using real humans Caroline Broder , a partner at Base10 Partners who led the investment, said Throxy's focus on underserved industries represents a massive market opportunity that established players have largely ignored. "The market is almost laughably large — even just focusing on US and EU businesses in a couple of traditional industries like manufacturing, logistics, and distribution results in hundreds of thousands of companies with a real willingness to buy," Broder told VentureBeat. What sets Throxy apart is not just its data sources but its business model. Rather than selling software licenses or charging monthly fees, the company operates on a pay-for-results basis. Clients only pay when Throxy books qualified meetings with genuine prospects. "What is a qualified meeting for you? Forget what we think. What is it for you?" Jiménez de Parga explained. "Whatever that qualified meeting is for you is what we'll adhere to, and that's why we never have problems." This approach addresses a longstanding misalignment in sales organizations, where marketing-qualified leads often fail to convert and sales development representatives clash with account executives over lead quality. By tying payment directly to outcomes, Throxy forces itself to maintain rigorous standards while giving clients predictable returns on investment. The model appears to be working. Imnoo , which makes AI-powered quoting software for computer numerical control manufacturers, reported generating three to five qualified meetings per week consistently after partnering with Throxy. "The manufacturing industry is one of the toughest markets to crack — it's complex and relationship driven," said Niklas Gerlach, Imnoo's chief operating officer. "With Throxy as our partner, we're starting real conversations with prospects we know will be interested." Small startup takes on Salesforce and HubSpot Throxy's approach puts it in direct competition with established giants like Salesforce , HubSpot and newer AI-powered entrants that have raised hundreds of millions in venture funding. But Broder argues that incumbents face structural disadvantages in addressing traditional industries. "Incumbents like Salesforce and HubSpot are wed to their seat-based pricing model, both in how they charge customers, but also in how they build product," she said. "From a technical perspective, they are building AI features on top of their core, but have not built the product to support that from the ground up." The founders' contrarian stance extends to their view of the broader AI sales automation trend. In a blog post titled " AI SDRs Are Killing Sales ," Jiménez de Parga argued that most AI sales tools create more noise than value, contributing to email saturation that makes it harder for legitimate outreach to break through. "The rise of AI tools has unleashed a flood of content, automation, and accessibility, saturating every digital space with endless streams of information," he wrote. "The industry may, ironically, be worsening the very problem it set out to solve." This philosophy translates into Throxy's operational approach. While the company uses artificial intelligence for data processing and lead qualification, human experts craft all outreach messages and manage client relationships. The company describes itself as providing " Service-as-a-Software " rather than traditional Software-as-a-Service. Can a human-first sales model actually scale? The challenge facing Throxy is whether its high-touch, human-centric approach can scale efficiently enough to justify venture capital investment. Traditional software companies can serve thousands of customers with relatively small teams, but service businesses typically require linear scaling of human resources. Jiménez de Parga addresses this concern by pointing to the company's track record of reaching $1.5 million in revenue with three people — a feat accomplished by using their own platform to generate all of the company's sales pipeline. "We use our own product extensively. We have never spent money on ads because we believe all of our pipeline should be generated by our own product," he said. "If we can't generate leads for ourselves, how can we do it well for our customers?" The company plans to use its new funding to expand headcount by nearly five times, focusing on hiring additional human experts who can manage larger portfolios of clients while maintaining personalization quality. Base10's Broder said she's not concerned about scalability challenges. "This is a forcing function for the business to find product-market fit and build something people want faster," she explained. "Tying revenue to results puts a lot of confidence in the team and in the product." Pay-for-results pricing shakes up sales software Throxy's success could signal a broader shift in enterprise sales technology, where the pendulum swings back toward human expertise augmented by artificial intelligence rather than AI attempting to replace human judgment entirely. This trend aligns with growing customer fatigue over automated outreach. Research suggests that positive reply rates for cold emails have declined significantly as AI-powered tools flood inboxes with generic messages that recipients can easily identify as automated. "I think we're seeing a lot of AI agents, but there's not a lot of AI agents replying to these," Jiménez de Parga predicted. "I think there's going to start becoming, at some point, that there's going to be some sort of AI negotiation." For traditional industries specifically, the implications could be profound. Manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and other sectors have historically lagged in technology adoption, creating opportunities for companies that can bridge the digital divide with human expertise. The pay-for-results model may also gain traction more broadly as companies face pressure to demonstrate clear returns on marketing and sales investments. In an economic environment where customer acquisition costs continue rising, outcome-based pricing offers a way to align vendor incentives with customer success. Throxy graduated from Y Combinator's Spring 2025 cohort alongside companies like 11x , which raised $50 million for AI sales development representatives — representing the exact opposite approach to sales automation. As both companies scale, they'll test competing visions for the future of enterprise sales. The winner may determine whether the next generation of sales technology amplifies human capabilities or attempts to replace them entirely. If Throxy succeeds, it could prove that in the age of artificial intelligence, the most disruptive innovation is putting humans back in charge.
